title: Evaluating a Generate–Validate–Repair Pipeline for LLM‑based Network Configuration: a Paired, Emulation‑Grounded Study
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired, emulation‑grounded experiment (study id study-cand-1-gvr-verifier-adversarial-2026-08-01) to test whether integrating a deterministic network verifier into a generate–validate–repair (GVR) pipeline reduces the rate of unsafe configuration applications from an LLM relative to an LLM‑only pipeline. The primary estimand is the absolute paired difference in unsafe_apply rate (guarded − baseline) where unsafe_apply = 1 indicates a final configuration that would cause a semantic safety violation. We ran N = 240 paired intent→configuration tasks (144 in‑distribution, 48 distribution‑shift, 48 adversarial) using the declared model gpt-5-mini and a deterministic validator; execution followed shared_initial_candidate semantics (one shared LLM generation per task reused across arms). All archived scoring artifacts report safe outcomes for every paired episode: baseline_safe = 240/240 and guarded_safe = 240/240. The paired risk difference = 0.00 with bootstrap 95% percentile CI [0.00, 0.00] (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729) and exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. Critically, under the preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics the guarded arm could only change the paired outcome if the single shared candidate failed deterministic validation and triggered a repair; in this run no such failures nor repairs occurred, rendering the paired contrast degenerate. We report the preregistered design, artifact‑grounded execution accounting, quantitative analysis, an artifact‑grounded failure analysis explaining the null paired outcome, and concrete recommendations for future informative GVR evaluations.

sections.introduction: Translating operator intent into device configurations that preserve ordering, dependencies, and invariants is a central NetOps challenge. Large language models (LLMs) offer flexible intent‑to‑configuration translation, but text‑centric evaluation masks semantic execution failures (ordering mistakes, transient invariants, protected‑resource touches) that only appear when configurations are applied in an execution environment. Closed‑loop, emulation‑grounded evaluation addresses this gap by deterministically applying generated configurations to device images or simulators and scoring resultant network states for semantic safety. A common mitigation pattern is generate–validate–repair (GVR): an LLM produces a candidate, a deterministic verifier checks invariants, and an automated repair step rewrites the candidate when violations are detected. Prior work demonstrates the feasibility of GVR patterns in configuration and program repair domains and motivates empirical tests under distribution shift and adversarial inputs. This study reports a fully preregistered paired evaluation that measured a single, well‑defined estimand (paired difference in unsafe_apply rate) using an emulation‑grounded scorer and shared_initial_candidate execution semantics. Our contributions are: (1) an artifact‑grounded presentation of a preregistered paired GVR test (study id study-cand-1-gvr-verifier-adversarial-2026-08-01); (2) exact numeric mapping from archived analysis artifacts to the primary estimand; and (3) a failure analysis explaining the null paired result plus concrete, evidence‑based recommendations for future informative designs.
sections.related_work: Executable, emulation‑grounded NetOps benchmarks have recently emerged to surface workflow and planning faults rather than only textual fidelity; NetConfArena is an example of this closed‑loop approach [1]. Automatic configuration repair and program repair literature documents generate–validate patterns and high repair coverage for many syntactic and some semantic faults, while noting that verifier semantic coverage varies by design and domain [2],[4]. Surveys and position papers synthesize agentic architectures, tool augmentation, verifier integration, and uncertainty calibration as relevant building blocks for safe NetOps automation [3],[5]. Engineering precedent from configuration analysis tools such as Batfish shows how verifier design and incremental verification can be operationalized at scale [6]. Our study differs by combining a predeclared paired estimand, shared_initial_candidate execution semantics, deterministic emulation scoring, and full archival of per‑call and validator traces to permit traceable reconciliation of numerical claims.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and estimand: We preregistered the study (study id study-cand-1-gvr-verifier-adversarial-2026-08-01). The primary estimand is paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline, the absolute paired difference in unsafe_apply rate where unsafe_apply = 1 indicates a final configuration that would cause a semantic safety violation when applied. The analysis procedures (paired contingency table, bootstrap CI, McNemar exact test) and sensitivity treatments (exclusions for verifier–simulator inconsistency and infra failures) were fixed before execution.

Design and sampling: The design is paired with shared_initial_candidate generation semantics (the adapter produced exactly one initial LLM generation per task and both arms used that same generation). We executed N = 240 distinct intent→configuration tasks, blocked into topology/vendor clusters and composed as: in‑distribution 60% (144 tasks), distribution‑shift 20% (48 tasks), and adversarial‑prompt 20% (48 tasks). Task generation used a deterministic task generator that emitted canonical intent payloads, initial states, required sequences, and constraints; representative task manifests and difficulty labels ("very_hard"/"extreme") are archived.

Model, verifier, and adapter contract: Execution used the declared model gpt-5-mini and a deterministic network verifier under a hosted adapter family implementing shared_initial_candidate semantics; the guarded pipeline was permitted up to one validator‑triggered repair per task. Under shared_initial_candidate semantics, a single shared LLM candidate per task is produced and reused across the paired baseline and guarded episodes; therefore a paired divergence can arise only if that shared candidate fails deterministic validation and the guarded arm applies a repair that changes the final configuration.

Scoring and exclusions: A deterministic emulation scorer assigned a binary final outcome: safe (0) or unsafe (1) based on invariant checks after applying the final configuration to the emulator. Preregistered exclusions included items flagged as 'possible false‑safe' (validator PASS but emulator unsafe outcome) and unrecoverable infra failures after the retry policy; sensitivity analyses were defined to treat excluded pairs as unsafe. The retry policy allowed up to two infra recovery attempts per episode.

Analysis procedures: The primary analysis used a paired contingency table for discordant pairs, a bootstrap percentile CI for the paired risk difference (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729), and an exact two‑sided McNemar test on discordant counts. Secondary analyses planned to report repair‑iteration counts, model‑call budgets, and per‑condition summaries. All analysis parameters and outputs were archived and are traceable to the execution and analysis artifacts.
sections.results:
Execution accounting: The run completed according to the preregistered plan. Planned episodes = 480; completed episodes = 480; complete paired tasks = 240. The provider call audit recorded exactly one initial generation per task and model_calls_used = 240 consistent with shared_initial_candidate semantics. No infra failures occurred and no preregistered exclusions were invoked.

Primary binary outcomes: Every paired episode was scored safe under both arms. The condition summary reports baseline_successes = 240, baseline_failures = 0, guarded_successes = 240, guarded_failures = 0. The paired contingency is n11 (both safe) = 240; n10 = 0; n01 = 0; n00 = 0. The paired estimator (guarded_unsafe_rate − baseline_unsafe_rate) = 0.00. Bootstrap percentile 95% CI = [0.00, 0.00] (resamples = 10,000, seed = 1729). Exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0.

Validator activity and repair utilization: Archived validator traces show validation metadata (observed touched field counts, required command counts, difficulty labels) and indicate that every shared initial candidate passed deterministic validation; consequently, no validator‑triggered repairs were applied and repair_attempts = 0. Because the guarded final configurations matched the shared initial candidate for every episode, baseline and guarded outcomes are identical across all subgroups (in‑distribution, distribution‑shift, adversarial), producing degenerate subgroup contrasts.

Unused sensitivity channels: The preregistration included planned sensitivity analyses for 'possible false‑safe' flags and infra failures. None occurred, so those sensitivity channels remained unused. Representative archived traces support these findings and record the recorded analysis parameters (bootstrap resamples and seed) used to compute the reported CI.
sections.discussion:
Artifact‑grounded explanation for the null paired contrast: Under shared_initial_candidate semantics the adapter produced a single LLM output per task that both arms used. The guarded arm could only change the paired outcome by detecting a violation in that shared candidate and applying the preregistered repair routine. In this run the deterministic validator passed every shared candidate and no repairs were invoked; hence there were zero discordant pairs. This mechanistic account is supported by the execution accounting (one shared initial generation per task) and validator traces (all PASS), and it explains the degenerate statistical outcome (estimate = 0.0, CI = [0.0,0.0], p = 1.0).

Design implications and recommendations for informative GVR evaluation: The observed degeneracy highlights three design levers to create informative paired contrasts: (1) generation semantics — permit independent initial generations per arm (remove shared_initial_candidate) so the guarded pipeline can be tested against an unguarded generator sample; (2) adversary and perturbation strength — increase adversarial challenge (adaptive adversaries, multiple seeds, or stronger perturbations) to generate more initial candidates that fail deterministic checks; (3) repair expressiveness — allow iterative repair budgets and richer repair strategies so the repair mechanism can be exercised and its effect quantified. Each recommendation directly follows from archived provider/audit and validator activity showing identical shared outputs and zero repair usage.

Threats to validity: Internal validity — the shared_initial_candidate execution contract was a deliberate design choice that limits causal contrast interpretation; this constraint was preregistered and adhered to at runtime. Construct validity — the deterministic verifier implements a finite check set; while validator traces report many observables, uncovered semantic fault classes may remain. External validity — tasks were drawn from a NetConfArena‑style synthetic emulation corpus; extrapolation to production, multi‑vendor deployments requires caution. Conclusion validity — the observed baseline unsafe rate = 0 prevents detection of verifier benefit in this design; future power planning should account for generator variability and adversary strength to ensure nondegenerate discordant counts.

Operational implications: The experiment shows that when initial LLM candidates systematically satisfy deterministic checks, a verifier can produce no measurable marginal benefit in a paired shared‑candidate design. Operational evaluations of GVR pipelines should therefore ensure the evaluation design permits the verifier and repair components to operate on nontrivial failure cases if the goal is to estimate causal verifier impact.
sections.conclusion: We executed a fully preregistered, emulation‑grounded paired evaluation of a GVR pipeline for LLM‑based network configuration. All 240 paired tasks were scored safe under both the LLM‑only and the guarded arms, yielding a paired difference of 0.00 (bootstrap 95% CI [0.00,0.00]; McNemar p = 1.0). This degenerate outcome is artifact‑grounded: under the preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics the single shared initial candidate per task passed deterministic validation in every case, and no repairs were invoked, so the guarded arm had no opportunity to produce discordant outcomes. We present the preregistered design, numerical mapping to archived analysis outputs, an artifact‑grounded failure analysis, and concrete recommendations (alter generation semantics, raise adversarial strength, and increase repair expressiveness) for future experiments that seek informative estimates of verifier benefit. The archived execution and analysis artifacts support independent reconciliation of the numeric claims and the conclusions reported here.

disclosure_statement: Declared model and tools: execution used the hosted model declared as gpt-5-mini via the registered adapter family hosted_netops_gvr_v1; the guarded pipeline employed a deterministic network verifier identified as deterministic_netops_validator_v5 and permitted up to one validator‑triggered repair per task. Preregistration and autonomy: the study was preregistered (study id study-cand-1-gvr-verifier-adversarial-2026-08-01; preregistration SHA‑256: 3e73ca0dc935a8754bf2dfbe6869ff989c47f1db0d93e2ca34809be8ebf95e26) and executed under the frozen plan after the autonomy lock. Autonomy boundary and human role: prior to the lock the human Research Director selected the topic family and constrained the initial master prompt; thereafter literature search, experiment selection, preregistration, execution, analysis, manuscript drafting, and revision were performed autonomously. Shared‑candidate semantics: the registered adapter used shared_initial_candidate semantics (one shared initial generation per task reused across both arms); under that contract a paired divergence could only arise if the shared candidate failed deterministic validation or if a validator‑triggered repair was applied. Artifact archive pointer: the complete execution and analysis bundle (execution manifest, per‑call traces, task manifests, validator traces, and analysis artifacts) is archived and available for reconciliation with the numeric claims reported here. Immutable master prompt reference: the initial master prompt is archived (provenance locator and SHA‑256 reference retained in the archive). No manual human editing of technical manuscript content occurred after the autonomy lock.
limitations: Emulator and corpus scope: tasks used a NetConfArena‑style synthetic emulation corpus; external validity to production, multi‑vendor networks and operator workflows is limited.
Single model: the study exercised a single hosted model (gpt-5-mini); results do not imply generality across other models, prompts, or prompting strategies.

Shared_initial_candidate semantics: the paired design used one shared initial generation per task; this prevented generator variability between arms and made verifier benefit contingent on initial candidate failures.
Adversary bounds: adversarial prompts were generated under a preregistered, fixed adversary protocol and do not represent unconstrained, adaptive adversaries.

Verifier coverage: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 implements a finite rule set; uncovered semantic fault classes may remain undetected, and planned detector cross‑checks remain an area for extension.
